Package 0.2: Freeze the demo as v1 (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
The tag demo-v1 and a note in the demo's README that it is the frozen reference. Done when git tag -l demo-v1 prints it, docs/product-demo/README.md says 'Demo v1', and python docs/product-demo/build.py --check passes.

The request: Keep the redesigned demo as demo v1, the agreed reference for development: the product must look and behave exactly like it, and nobody edits the demo from now on.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Keep the redesigned demo as demo v1, the agreed reference for development: the product must look and behave exactly like it, and nobody edits the demo from now on.

(2) Plan
1. Add a 'Demo v1: frozen reference for development' note to docs/product-demo/README.md.
2. Tag the demo commit as demo-v1 with an annotated message.
3. Keep the demo's build --check inside make rd-check so it stays buildable.
4. Ask the owner before pushing main, dev and the tag; push once approved.

(3) Decisions
- The product frontend is a copy of the demo, never the demo itself. Because: The frozen demo is the yardstick; editing it would remove the reference the product is compared against.
- Pushing waited for the owner's explicit yes. Because: A push changes the shared repository; the package prompt asks for approval first.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Someone edits docs/product-demo to change the product, and the reference moves with the thing it should measure.
- A lightweight tag carries no statement of what it freezes; an annotated tag with a message does.
- The demo stops building as its sources age, so the reference can no longer be opened; build --check in rd-check guards that.
- Pushing main, dev and the tag without the owner's yes changes the shared repository.
- Later fixes (the phone-width top bar, the fonts) applied to the demo as well, so the frozen copy no longer shows what was agreed.

Package 1.1: Copy the demo into the product frontend, with a build (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
dclab_rnd/agentic/web/src/ (shell, styles, core, one view file per page) and web/build.py writing separate files into dclab_rnd/agentic/static/app/. Done when the build's --check says the frontend is up to date and tests/test_web_build.py passes.

The request: Build the real product with exactly the demo's UI, UX and frontend, and make it work for real with a backend; change nothing in the UI unless the owner asks.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Build the real product with exactly the demo's UI, UX and frontend, and make it work for real with a backend; change nothing in the UI unless the owner asks.

(2) Plan
1. Explore the backend, the current web UI and the demo frontend in parallel to see what the product can reuse.
2. Copy docs/product-demo/src into dclab_rnd/agentic/web/src without changing its look.
3. Write build.py: assemble index.html, app.css and one JavaScript file per view and data file into static/app, nothing inlined.
4. Add --check (exit 1 when static/app is stale or has extra files), a make web target, and the check inside make rd-check.
5. Serve it on a test server with a temporary data folder and compare screenshots with demo v1.

(3) Decisions
- The build writes separate files instead of one self-contained page. Because: The server's Content-Security-Policy allows no inline scripts or styles, so a single inlined page like the demo's would be blocked.
- static/app is generated and checked for freshness in rd-check. Because: A hand edit to generated output would silently drift from the sources.
- A test server with a temporary DCLAB_AGENT_HOME, never the owner's running notebook. Because: The owner's make notebook on port 8765 holds real projects that a check must not touch.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The demo's build inlines every script and style into one page; under the server's CSP, which allows no inline code, a straight copy would render blank.
- A hand edit to the generated static/app drifts from web/src without anyone noticing.
- Checking against the owner's running notebook on port 8765 could touch real projects.
- Pages still carry the demo's sample numbers after the copy and can be mistaken for real results.
- A copy step can change the look slightly (fonts, spacing) in a way only a side-by-side screenshot shows.

(5) How you will know it is done
- look parity with demo v1: Every page served by the real server under the strict CSP renders the same as demo v1, with no console error.

Package 1.2: No inline styles or scripts (strict CSP) (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
Per-element styles written as data-style and applied by core.js through one constructed stylesheet; the build fails on any inline script, style block, on... handler or style attribute. Done when the build tests pass, including the one that catches an inline style, and every page renders as demo v1.

The request: Serve the demo's UI under the server's strict Content-Security-Policy without changing how any page looks.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Serve the demo's UI under the server's strict Content-Security-Policy without changing how any page looks.

(2) Plan
1. Find every inline style attribute in the views and in strings built by JavaScript (102 of them).
2. Rewrite each as data-style and teach core.js to turn each distinct value into one rule of a constructed stylesheet, watching for new values with a MutationObserver.
3. Add a global [hidden]{display:none!important} rule.
4. Make build.py refuse inline scripts, style blocks, event-handler attributes and style attributes, and test that.
5. Compare every page with demo v1 at 1440 px.

(3) Decisions
- data-style plus a constructed stylesheet ([data-style="..."]:not([hidden]){...}) instead of utility classes or setting el.style from script. Because: CSSOM rules are not blocked by the CSP, the page looks the same, and pages that re-render with innerHTML stay CSP-clean without extra code.
- The build refuses inline code rather than relying on a review. Because: One forgotten style= attribute breaks a page silently under the CSP; a build error catches it at once.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Inline styles hide inside JavaScript strings as well as markup, so a search of the views alone misses some of them.
- Rules generated from data-style lose to component classes unless they keep the priority an inline style had.
- A generated rule can un-hide an element the page hid with the hidden attribute.
- Markup added later through innerHTML carries data-style values no rule exists for, unless new values are watched.
- Without a refusal in the build, a new style= attribute breaks a page silently under the CSP.

The demo relied on a rule its viewer added; served on its own the page lacked it.

(2) Why it matters
On the product's own Home, outside the viewer that had supplied the rule, elements the page hid stayed on screen whenever their class set a display. It changes what DCLab does for a person without anyone deciding it: a result, a refusal or an artefact differs from what the person was promised, silently.

(3) The smallest fix
A global [hidden]{display:none!important} rule, and data-style rules written with :not([hidden]) so a style never un-hides an element.

(4) The test that proves it
No dedicated test was recorded for this fix: write one that reproduces the scenario above and fails before the change.

(5) What stays open
Nothing beyond the scenario, once the test passes.

What the package must deliver:

Plan the work.

- Admitting Google Fonts in the CSP opens the policy to an outside host, and a loose edit could admit more.
- The old UI's files under /static and the new app's under /static/app could shadow each other.

Package 1.5: Serve the fonts from the app (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
Inter, JetBrains Mono and Vazirmatn as variable woff2 files under web/src/fonts (SIL Open Font License, licence texts beside them); no request to any other host. Done when the build tests pass: no outside host in the page, the stylesheet or the CSP, and every @font-face file is shipped.

The request: The page should contact no other host: a page load told Google that someone opened the workspace, which sits badly next to 'data stays on this machine', and the UI lost its fonts offline. Ask before downloading any font file.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The page should contact no other host: a page load told Google that someone opened the workspace, which sits badly next to 'data stays on this machine', and the UI lost its fonts offline. Ask before downloading any font file.

(2) Plan
1. Ask the owner before downloading Inter and Vazirmatn (about 1 MB, OFL); JetBrains Mono was already on the machine.
2. Subset the local JetBrains Mono to woff2 and take the Latin and Arabic subsets of the other two (about 268 KB in all).
3. Declare them with @font-face under the same family names so the look does not change.
4. Make the build copy binary files and compare them in --check; remove the Google hosts from the CSP.
5. Test that nothing loads from another host and that every named font is shipped; check all 19 pages in a browser.

(3) Decisions
- Latin-extended and Arabic files load only when a page uses those characters. Because: Most pages need only Latin; unicode-range keeps the first load small while Persian text still renders.
- The test inspects what the page loads (link, script, img, @import, url()), not every URL in its text. Because: The page legitimately mentions URLs as text and placeholders; only loaded resources contact a host.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Downloading font files without asking breaks the owner's rule to approve every download.
- Self-hosted fonts under other family names or weights would change the look of every page.
- Shipping Arabic and Latin-extended glyphs on every page slows the first load for pages that never use them.
- A test that searches the page text for URLs fails on harmless placeholders, and people learn to ignore it.
- The build copied text files only; binary woff2 files could go missing or stale without its check noticing.

(5) How you will know it is done

(1) What the package is for
server.py holds most routes as closures and reads the environment in many places. Introduce one settings object read once, split the routes into routers per area that receive their dependencies through FastAPI Depends, and give every route pydantic request and response models, keeping every path, status code and payload as it is.

(2) Plan
1. Check which tests depend on exact error text and when the tests set the model key, so reading settings once per app is safe.
2. Write settings.py; read empty variables as unset.
3. Move the routes into routers (core, research runs, projects, intern and lessons; the drafts in draft/api.py; each page in agentic/pages) that take the stores, the gateway and the running jobs through Depends(services).

The request: Background work runs as asyncio tasks inside the server: a restart loses it, leaves projects stuck 'running', and nothing can stop it. Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Background work runs as asyncio tasks inside the server: a restart loses it, leaves projects stuck 'running', and nothing can stop it. Make stage runs, data pipelines, synthetic data and intern sessions rows in a job table run by workers, with progress, cancel, retry and recovery after a restart.

(2) Plan
1. Map every background task the server starts (an explore agent).
2. Write the job store on files (jobs.json under a lock) and PostgreSQL (the job table, migration 0009, one queued or running job per key by a partial unique index).
3. Write the control (checkpoint, progress) and a worker with one dispatcher thread, heartbeats every 5 s and recovery of stale jobs; handlers for the four kinds.
4. Move the draft work out of the route closures, queue jobs from the routes, add checkpoints between stages, pipeline steps, intern tool calls and synthetic design and generation.
5. Add the jobs API (list, read, Stop, Retry) and the buttons on the Compute page; run the worker as its own process under make dev.
6. Check the Done when by hand: kill a real server with SIGKILL mid-run on files and on PostgreSQL, start it again, retry; then two API instances and a separate worker on one database.
7. Gate and reviewer; three review rounds; commit.

(3) Decisions
- A stop takes effect at the next checkpoint between steps; a stage is never cut. Because: A stage must stay deterministic: same seed, same record. Cutting a stage mid-fit would leave half a record.
- One queued or running job per key, enforced by a unique index. Because: Two app instances must never start the same project's stages; only the database can decide that for both.
- A running job is interrupted only while its heartbeat is still stale, and a worker whose job was taken stops and writes nothing more. Because: Recovery must never take a job from a live worker or let the displaced worker damage the run that took over (findings F1 and R1).
- Job responses leave out the free text a payload carries. Because: An intern message or a prompt for a model is user text; the API strips it as it already strips session messages.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Recovery could take a job from a worker that is alive but slow, and both would run it.
- Cutting a stage mid-fit would leave half a record and break the rule that a stage is deterministic.
- Two app instances could start the same project's stages unless the database alone decides.
- A by-hand crash test could pass because a leftover server on the same port did the work.
- Job rows carry user text (intern messages, prompts to a model) that an API could return.

(5) How you will know it is done
- kill the server mid-run, then start it again: Killing the server mid-run and starting it again resumes or cleanly fails the job, and Retry runs it (the package's Done when).

Review it.

(1) Findings
- F7 [privacy] The job API returned free text.
  Scenario: GET /api/jobs returned payload.text (the user's intern message) and payload.prompt (text sent to the synthetic-schema model).
  Why it matters: GET /api/jobs returned the user's intern messages and the text sent to the synthetic-schema model to anyone who could list jobs.
  Fix to ask for: A public view drops text and prompt in list, read, stop and retry.
- F1 [behaviour] Recovery could interrupt a job whose worker was still alive, and that worker never noticed.
  Scenario: Worker A's heartbeat goes stale (a database outage, a debugger, a laptop asleep under make dev); worker B's recovery marks the job interrupted and settles it; a person retries and B claims it; A keeps running through every later checkpoint, so A and B run the same stage job on one project at once, and whichever finishes first marks it done.
  Why it matters: When a live worker's heartbeat went stale (a laptop asleep, a database blip), two workers could run the same stage job on one project at once, their steps interleaved, and the first to finish marked the job done while the other still wrote to the project.
  Fix to ask for: interrupt takes older_than and requires the heartbeat to still be that old; Control.check stops a job whose row is no longer running or no longer this worker's; finish and progress are no-ops for another worker.
- F3 [behaviour] make dev relied on watchfiles, which no requirements file installs.
  Scenario: On a fresh .venv from requirements/base.txt the worker subprocess exits with 'No module named watchfiles'; the API runs with DCLAB_WORKER=external, so every stage run, pipeline and intern turn stays queued for ever, silently.
  Why it matters: On a fresh environment the worker of make dev exited at once while the API waited for an external worker, so every stage run, pipeline and intern turn stayed queued for ever with no error anywhere.
  Fix to ask for: worker_command() falls back to running the worker without reload, and a watcher thread warns loudly if the worker exits while the API runs.
- F5 [behaviour] No recovery on start after a quick restart.
  Scenario: A server killed and restarted within 120 s leaves its job running: the project shows running, new runs get 409, and a Stop does nothing for up to about three minutes until the periodic recovery runs.
  Why it matters: After a quick restart a job stayed 'running' for up to about three minutes: the project showed running, new runs got 409, and Stop did nothing.
  Fix to ask for: A running job whose worker was a process of this machine that has ended (a dead pid) is interrupted at once, provided its heartbeat is at least 15 s old.
- F6 [behaviour] A project was marked queued before the job insert, which could lose the race for the job key.
  Scenario: Instance A queues the final stage while instance B's run-all passes its active check in the same window: B overwrites data to models as queued, wiping their completed status, then gets 409, and those stages stay queued for good.
  Why it matters: With two app instances, a run that lost the race for the job key reset completed stages to queued and left them there for good, so finished results looked as if they had never run.
  Fix to ask for: mark_queued returns a snapshot that start_job and retry restore on ActiveJob; the pipeline retry checks for an active job first.
- R1 [behaviour] After the F1 fix, a worker that lost its job still settled it on top of the new owner's live run.
  Scenario: A goes stale, B recovers and later claims the retried job; A reaches a checkpoint and stops, then settles again: B's current stage becomes failed ('Interrupted'), its remaining stages go back to pending and the project's running field is cleared while B keeps executing.
  Why it matters: After the F1 fix, the displaced worker's tidy-up still marked the new owner's current stage failed, reset its waiting stages to pending and cleared the project's running field while the new owner kept executing, so the page showed a broken run that was in fact going on.
  Fix to ask for: Control records that the job was lost; execute skips settling and the stage handler tidies only when the job is still this worker's. A last gap (taken over during its last stage, so no later checkpoint) was closed with Control.owned(), checked before tidying.
- R2 [behaviour] The dead-pid recovery could interrupt a live job in another container with the same host name.
  Scenario: Two containers report the same hostname with separate process namespaces: os.kill(pid, 0) on the other container's live worker raises ProcessLookupError, so its job beating every 5 s is interrupted at once.
  Why it matters: Two containers sharing a host name would interrupt each other's live jobs at once, each taking the other's worker for a dead process.
  Fix to ask for: The dead-pid path also requires a heartbeat at least max(3 beats, 15 s) old.
- F4 [gap] No Stop button during the pipeline phase of a synthetic-data job.
  Scenario: Once the synthetic asset exists, its Compute row looks up a pipeline job keyed by draft and asset, which does not exist because the pipeline runs inside the synthetic job; the page offers no Stop though the job would honour one.
  Why it matters: While a synthetic-data job ran its pipeline, Compute offered no Stop, so a user could not stop work the job would have honoured.
  Fix to ask for: A draft's pipeline row falls back to the active synthetic job.
- F2 [flaky] The intern retry test failed under load.
  Scenario: After Retry the test waited 20 s for the retried turn to run the whole standard plan with five real stages; it failed three times out of three with three copies in parallel and twice during check-all, while passing alone in 12 to 16 s.
  Why it matters: The retry test failed under the parallel gate on a loaded machine, so check-all went red over a test that waited on real work instead of the state it checked.
  Fix to ask for: After Retry the test waits for attempts == 2, stops the job and waits for it to end.
- T3 [flaky] The takeover test failed once under load (status done, not running), found while reviewing 10.4.
  Scenario: Between the test's Retry and the second worker's claim, the worker under test, polling every 50 ms, claimed the job back.
  Why it matters: The test of the most delicate race, a takeover, failed once under load because the worker under test claimed the job back, so it could fail for a race in itself.
  Fix to ask for: The test hands the job to the other worker in one step.

(2) Verdict
FAIL: 10 findings to fix before this change is committed.

The request: With several app instances behind a load balancer, the chat and pipeline streams, the per-draft agent turn lock and the model pause must work when requests land on different instances.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
With several app instances behind a load balancer, the chat and pipeline streams, the per-draft agent turn lock and the model pause must work when requests land on different instances.

(2) Plan
1. Map what 9.2 already provides on PostgreSQL (numbered event rows, the advisory turn lock, row-locked writes) and what still assumes one process (the stream's poll, the busy check, the model pause in module memory).
2. Check that reply runs inside the turn lock and that the installed psycopg supports waiting for notifications with a timeout.
3. Send pg_notify in the transaction that writes each draft event; one listener thread per server process wakes the streams waiting on that draft; keep the 2-second poll as the fallback.
4. Make 'the agent is still answering' (409) ask the shared turn lock as well as this instance's queued turn.
5. Move the model pause to a model_pause row with an expiry (migration 0011), keyed by endpoint, model and a hash of the API key.
6. Test with two server processes and one worker process on one database; gate and reviewer; fix; commit.

(3) Decisions
- A notice only wakes a stream; the stream still reads the rows and replays from Last-Event-ID. Because: A missed notice then only delays a stream to its poll, never loses an event.
- The pause key includes a hash of the API key. Because: A new key must not stay paused by the old key's refusal, and the key itself must never be stored.
- A turn's user message and its answer are written under the turn lock. Because: That, not the 409 check, is what guarantees two messages never interleave across instances.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A stream that trusts notices alone loses an event whenever a notice is missed; the event rows must stay the source of truth and the poll the fallback.
- Turning the in-memory busy check into an awaited database probe can split a check-then-act on the event loop and let two turns in.
- LISTEN needs a long-lived direct connection and a driver that can wait with a timeout; a pooler or an older psycopg can disable it without any error.
- The shared model pause must key on something that changes with the API key without ever storing the key.
- A test with two server processes and a worker is heavy on an 8 GB machine; it can time out, and with output discarded it fails without a clue.

1. Read how the gateway enforces its spending caps and what each usage row records.
2. (1) What the package is for
In the live check, a small local model answered the Home conversation in prose and never called a tool, so nothing was recorded and the chat stopped. Make the conversation keep moving whatever the model does: the user must always have a next step.

(2) Plan
1. Run the Home conversation against the local Ollama model (qwen2.5-coder:1.5b) after the OpenAI account refused every request for lack of credit, and see where it stalls.
2. Pull the 'record the answer, mark the question answered, redraw the workflow, ask the next thing' block out of script_turn into one take_answer method, so the script and the model path share it.

- Small models often answer in prose and never call a tool; a conversation driven only by tool calls stalls on them.

- Code and model must not both record the same answer or both ask the next question in one turn.
- Tests that assume the model's text is the last message of a turn break once code speaks after the model.

2. Write scripts/dev.py with three commands (serve, db-reset, test-db): a reachability check with a start hint, ensure_database (create if missing, drop first on reset, then upgrade), a polling frontend watcher, and uvicorn with reload and one worker.

(3) Decisions
- The frontend watcher polls file modification times with the standard library. Because: watchfiles is installed but not a declared requirement; polling 36 source files once a second costs nothing and adds no dependency.
- A reset or a create touches only a database named dclab_<letters, digits, _> on this machine; --remote is the explicit override. Because: A reset drops a database with force; a URL left in a shell or in .env could point at a shared server, so the name alone is not a safe guard.
- The authoritative host check asks the server itself (inet_server_addr) before anything is created or dropped, beside the early URL checks. Because: libpq takes the host from many places (the URL, its host and hostaddr query, PGHOST, PGHOSTADDR, a service file); only the server's own address covers all of them in one place.
- make dev reads .env the way the server does. Because: Otherwise the script and the server it starts can silently use different databases.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A reset command that drops a database is one exported variable away from dropping someone else's: the guard must check where the connection really goes, not only the name.

(2) Plan
1. Check that PostgreSQL's dump and restore tools are installed and match the server.
2. Write dclab_rnd/storage/backup.py: pg_dump in custom format without owners or grants, the workspace folder as files.tar.gz, and a manifest of the schema, rows per table, files and both archives' SHA-256; restore checks the archives first, goes only into an empty database and an empty folder, and compares rows and files after.

(3) Decisions
- Row counts and the dump come from one exported snapshot. Because: Counting after the dump let a row written in between make the manifest disagree with the backup.
- Restore goes only into an empty database and an empty folder and checks the archives first. Because: A restore must never write over data; a damaged archive must restore nothing.
- Retention deletes a raw file only for a ready asset, only when the file on disk still has the recorded hash, and by moving it aside atomically, checking, then removing it. Because: A failed asset's raw file is its only copy and may be retried; a file name can be uploaded again at any moment; moving aside first means a concurrent upload can be put back and two sweeps delete and audit a file once.
- The sweep runs hourly on its own worker thread, never in the heartbeat. Because: Hashing many large files can take longer than the stale-job limit, and a silent heartbeat makes another worker mark running jobs interrupted.
- Passwords and TLS options travel in the environment of pg_dump and pg_restore, never on a command line. Because: Command lines are visible to other processes, and dropping the TLS options would carry the whole database over an unverified connection.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Retention deletes people's raw data: any mistake about which file belongs to which asset deletes the wrong file, with no undo.
- Files and assets can share a name, be retried, or be in flight when the sweep runs; only a file whose hash still matches a finished, newest asset may go.
- A backup that skips files silently (links, vanished files, its own output) looks complete until the day it is restored.
- The dump and the file archive are taken at different moments; counts and files must come from one consistent point, or the check reports false differences.
- Backup tools take the server's address and TLS settings from the URL; any option dropped on the way can dump the wrong server or over an unverified connection.

Review it.

(1) Findings
- F7 [privacy] The first owner's password would end up in logs.
  Scenario: The README passed DCLAB_NEW_PASSWORD in a run-task override, which CloudTrail records in clear text and DescribeTasks returns; on Google Cloud an env value on the job sits in its spec and audit logs. The command also lacked the network configuration.
  Why it matters: The first owner's password, typed into the README's command, would have been stored in clear text in the cloud's audit trail and returned by the task description to anyone with read access to the account.
  Fix to ask for: An admin task definition and a Cloud Run job read the password from its own secret; the README's command includes the network configuration.
- F1 [behaviour] Scale-in stopped workers that were running jobs.
  Scenario: Three workers each run a 30-minute stage and nothing is queued; after 15 minutes the queue-empty alarm fires, ECS stops any task, and its job ends interrupted with nothing retrying it (the comment said the next worker would). On Google Cloud automatic mode scales in on CPU, so an intern turn waiting on a model looks idle.
  Why it matters: On AWS, a quiet queue after a burst would have stopped workers in the middle of 30-minute stage runs; those jobs ended interrupted and nothing retried them, so people would find half-run projects waiting for a manual retry. On Google Cloud an intern turn waiting on a model looked idle and could be scaled away.
  Fix to ask for: Publish active jobs (waiting plus running) and scale in only when that is zero; correct the comment.
- F3 [behaviour] The AWS job-failures alarm could never fire.
  Scenario: The collector sent dclab_job_failures_total only with its kind and status dimensions (NoDimensionRollup) while the alarm asked for no dimensions: 50 failed jobs and the alarm stays OK.
  Why it matters: On AWS, a wave of failing jobs would have left the failure alarm green, so the operator would learn of it from users rather than from the monitoring the package set up.
  Fix to ask for: Use ZeroAndSingleDimensionRollup.
- F4 [behaviour] An image built as the README said would not run on either cloud.
  Scenario: docker build on an Apple-silicon Mac makes an arm64 image; the Fargate tasks are X86_64 and Cloud Run runs only amd64, so tasks exit with 'exec format error', and ECR's immutable tags force a rebuild under a new name.
  Why it matters: The owner, building on an Apple-silicon Mac as the README said, would have pushed an image neither cloud can run; every task would exit at start, and the registry's immutable tags would force a rebuild under a new name before anything worked.
  Fix to ask for: docker build --platform linux/amd64 in the README.
- F5 [behaviour] A worker could start before the schema was migrated, and a rollback could leave no workers.
  Scenario: An image adds a migration; the worker service replaces its task first and the new worker exits (schema behind); if the circuit breaker rolls back, the old worker then refuses the app's newer schema, and no worker is left.
  Why it matters: A release with a migration could have left the product with no worker at all: the new worker refused the old schema, and after a rollback the old worker refused the new one, so every queued stage run waited indefinitely.
  Fix to ask for: The worker's command runs storage upgrade first, safe under the advisory lock.
- F8 [behaviour] On AWS the empty secrets were created in the same apply as the services.
  Scenario: Every task fails at start until each secret has a value; with the circuit breaker the first deployment is marked failed with nothing to roll back to, and filling the secrets afterwards starts nothing without a forced redeployment.
  Why it matters: The owner's very first apply on AWS would have failed: every task crashed for lack of secret values, the deployment had nothing to roll back to, and filling the secrets afterwards started nothing without a forced redeploy.
  Fix to ask for: The README gives three steps: create the secrets, fill them, then apply everything.
- R1 [behaviour] The scaler's leader connection was never checked again.
  Scenario: Cloud SQL maintenance or a failover drops every connection; the old leader keeps saying 'leader', another worker takes the lock, and both apply the rule, so the pool grows or shrinks by two at once.
  Why it matters: After a routine Cloud SQL maintenance window or a failover, two workers could both believe they lead the scaler, and the worker pool would grow or shrink two steps at a time, overshooting the queue in both directions.
  Fix to ask for: Each check runs select 1 on the held connection; on failure it closes, forgets it and tries the lock again.
- R2 [behaviour] A failed metric write also skipped scaling.
  Scenario: A lasting Cloud Monitoring problem (quota, rejected write, missing grant) raised before the scaler ran, so the pool never grew or shrank though the Admin API it needs was fine.
  Why it matters: A lasting problem writing metrics, such as a quota or a removed permission, would also have frozen the worker pool's size, even though the API the scaler actually needs was working.
  Fix to ask for: Counting, publishing and scaling in separate try blocks, each logged under its own message.
- R3 [behaviour] 'Scaling in never stops a running job' was not true on AWS.
  Scenario: With 3 workers and a minimum of 1, the alarm stays in ALARM and removes a worker every 300 s; a job claimed at minute 19.5 is not yet in the published count, so the minute-20 scale-in can stop the task that claimed it.
  Why it matters: The promise that scaling in never stops a running job was false on AWS: a job claimed in the last minute before a scale-in could have its worker stopped under it and end interrupted.
  Fix to ask for: A worker running a job holds ECS task scale-in protection, set when it becomes busy, refreshed every 2 hours, cleared when idle.
- R4 [behaviour] Task protection also held back worker deployments.
  Scenario: With a maximum of 100%, ECS cannot start a new worker until the protected old one stops; under steady load the old worker keeps claiming and renewing its protection, so the deployment may never finish while old worker code runs against the migrated schema.
  Why it matters: Under steady load a worker deployment might never finish, leaving old worker code running against a database already migrated for the new release.
  Fix to ask for: Maximum 200% so new workers start beside the old; an old worker compares its task definition with the service's current one, drains (claims nothing new), finishes its jobs, and then its protection clears.
- R5 [behaviour] A drained worker never undrained or exited, so a rolled-back deployment could leave no worker taking jobs.
  Scenario: A new image's workers fail to start; meanwhile every old worker sees itself superseded and drains; the breaker rolls back, the old tasks are current again but stay drained; in staging (max 2) nothing runs until someone restarts the service. A workspace opened after the drain also got an undrained worker.
  Why it matters: A failed release that ECS rolled back could leave every worker drained, so in staging no job would run at all until someone noticed and restarted the service by hand.
  Fix to ask for: Once drained and idle the worker process ends, and ECS starts whatever task definition is now current; every workspace's worker is drained on each tick.
- R6 [behaviour] A job claimed at the moment of the drain could be interrupted.
  Scenario: The dispatcher is inside claim() when the watch drains the worker, sees nothing in running, and ends the process; the just-claimed job stops at its first checkpoint as interrupted.
  Why it matters: A job claimed at the very moment its worker drained would start and then stop at its first checkpoint as interrupted, waiting for a person to retry it, which is the outcome R3 and R4 were built to prevent.
  Fix to ask for: has_work() counts a job as soon as it is claimed; the process ends only after two idle ticks in a row while drained.
- F9 [latent] Several Google Cloud workers could write the same queue-metric series.
  Scenario: The series was labelled by host name, which Cloud Run does not make unique; writes less than 5 seconds apart or out of order are rejected.
  Why it matters: Two Google Cloud workers sharing a host name would write the same metric series, and the cloud rejects writes that close together or out of order, so the queue numbers the scaler reads could be missing or stale.
  Fix to ask for: Read the instance id from the metadata server.
- F2 [gap] On Google Cloud the workers did not scale with the job queue.
  Scenario: scaling_mode AUTOMATIC scales on instance busyness; the queue metric fed only an alert, so a backlog of low-CPU jobs never added a worker, yet the package was marked done.
  Why it matters: On Google Cloud a backlog of low-CPU jobs, such as model calls, would never have added a worker, so the queue grew while the package's status said workers scale with it; the claim in the playbook was false for one of the two clouds.
  Fix to ask for: A MANUAL worker pool sized by a rule and a scaler with leader election, with the needed IAM on the pool; the README says the Admin API call is tested only against a stand-in.
- F6 [flaky] The migration-lock test was flaky in the parallel PostgreSQL run.
  Scenario: pg_locks lists locks for the whole cluster; other test processes take the same advisory key while migrating their own dclab_test_p<N>, so the holders seen become [2, 1, 1] and the test fails at random. It also never checked the threads' errors or a migration from empty.
  Why it matters: The test that proves only one instance migrates at a time failed at random in the parallel PostgreSQL run, so a real regression in the migration lock would have been dismissed as the usual flake.
  Fix to ask for: Filter pg_locks by the current database, collect thread errors, and migrate a scratch database from empty with three instances.

(2) Verdict

The request: The owner had a confidential delivery-fraud hiring challenge solved by hand outside the repository, then said it was a probe: DCLab itself must be able to solve problems like it. Start Part 4 with a replica of the challenge, invented end to end so the real files never enter the repository, and an acceptance test of the decisions DCLab must reach on it. Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner had a confidential delivery-fraud hiring challenge solved by hand outside the repository, then said it was a probe: DCLab itself must be able to solve problems like it. Start Part 4 with a replica of the challenge, invented end to end so the real files never enter the repository, and an acceptance test of the decisions DCLab must reach on it. Do not change the engine in this package.

(2) Plan
1. Read Part 4's lessons from the hand solution (labels joined on the wrong key, rows clustered on bikers, behaviour over raw columns, families compared under a rule, limits stated) and turn each into a trap to plant.
2. Write the generator as its own module (dclab_rnd/replicas/delivery_fraud.py): one seeded random generator, a facts dict computed from the data, and save() writing only the two files and a marker that they are synthetic.
3. Check the planted signal with the hand method: behaviour features with folds grouped by biker, against raw columns and against a random split that lets the model see the biker id.
4. Run the engine as it was on the replica, with the labels joined by hand, to record the baseline every later package must beat.
5. Write the acceptance tests, each marked expectedFailure with the package that must pass it, and run each without its marker to check it fails for its own reason.
6. Run make check-all and the dclab-reviewer; fix the six findings; re-measure the numbers on the new generator and record them in the playbook row.

(3) Decisions
- The replica is its own module, not a template in draft/synthetic.py. Because: The spec generator draws one table from a linear predictor; it cannot express two files, a join key that inflates labels, or behaviour across rows.
- Three customer accounts, not the two the text names. Because: A third small account keeps the (account, biker) join from being a plain two-way split, so the inflation it causes is realistic.
- Each acceptance test is marked expectedFailure and names the package that must make it pass. Because: Every later package turns one part green, and an unexpected success fails the suite, so the package that makes a test pass must also remove its marker.
- The end-to-end test asks for the decisions and a point AP above 0.35 and above 20 times chance, with the interval computed over bikers, not for the interval's lower end to clear chance. Because: A holdout grouped by biker holds only a handful of fraud bikers (4 to 11 in a simulation), and a good model's lower bound fell below chance on some holdouts; a test that can fail with a correct engine proves nothing.
- All vocabulary and formats in the replica are invented. Because: The challenge's data must not be disclosed or distributed; even label strings, category names, account ids or a phone format copied from it would leak it.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The confidential challenge files must never enter the repository, and nothing copied from them (labels, category names, ids, formats) may enter the replica either.
- A replica built by someone who knows the real solution can be shaped to fit it; the planted signal must be checked by the method, with the leak's flattering split shown too.
- An acceptance test that asserts on a noisy statistic (the lower end of an interval over few groups) can stay red with a correct engine.
- Acceptance tests that check that fields exist, rather than the decisions in them, would certify a wrong engine.
- Each expected failure must name the package that turns it green, or a test silently depends on work nobody planned.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted signal recoverable by the hand method: The planted signal must be recoverable by the hand solution's method (Done-when of 15.1): behaviour features with folds grouped by biker far above chance and above raw columns, and a random split with the biker id must flatter raw columns.
- the engine as it was, on the replica: No gate: a baseline for the end-to-end acceptance test (AP above 0.35).

  Scenario: The first generator planted 16 fraud bikers, 6 of them self-dealers whose frauds leave no trace in the table. A 20% holdout grouped by biker gets about 4 fraud bikers. The request: DCLab should solve many kinds of machine-learning problems, not only the three tasks it knows. Start with one interface every kind plugs into, and move binary, multiclass, regression and text + tabular onto it without changing behaviour.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
DCLab should solve many kinds of machine-learning problems, not only the three tasks it knows. Start with one interface every kind plugs into, and move binary, multiclass, regression and text + tabular onto it without changing behaviour.

(2) Plan
1. Count where the code branches on the task (runner 21, engine 17, benchmark 6, service 4, others) and decide which branches belong to a kind.
2. Before touching the engine, record the stage records of eight representative projects (HyperAck, Telco churn, letters multiclass, bike regression, clothing reviews text, the fraud replica with the imbalanced pack, the ticket and delivery replicas), twice, to learn the run-to-run noise.
3. Write the interface as a base class whose every part has a default, so a kind overrides only what differs; auto-register every module that defines KIND.
4. Move the per-task code (target encoding, text handling, machine, metrics and defaults, spec settings, target summary and claim, rare screen, model families) into the five built-in kinds.
5. Route the engine, Solution, prepare_bundle, exports and Home through the kind; add /api/kinds.
6. Re-run the eight projects and compare; write tests including a toy kind through all five stages; run the reviewer; fix; rd-check.

(3) Decisions
- The runner stays the machine layer keyed by task_type; a kind chooses the machine. Because: The runner's 57 task_type branches compute folds, fits and metrics for four numeric machines; moving them would risk behaviour for no gain until a kind needs a new machine (forecasting, survival), which then adds it in its own package.
- Text + tabular and rare events are kinds that inherit from binary. Because: They run on the binary machines and differ only in detection, defaults, questions and export; inheritance keeps the behaviour identical by construction.
- A pack's defaults (metric, rare-event screen) live in its kind. Because: A pack used to change only labels; through its kind it changes what runs, in one place.
- Parity is measured on stage records with ids and timings normalised, against two baseline runs. Because: Two runs of the unchanged code differed only in project ids, fit timings and one tie between tuning candidates, so any other difference after the change is real.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Moving the engine's task branches into kinds changes a stage record on a path the parity projects never exercise, such as a pack combined with a positive rate none of the replicas has.
- A pack's kind is applied to a project whose table it does not fit, so a project that exported or scored fine before is refused or scored differently.
- A kind declares baselines or checks that no stage computes, and /api/kinds then advertises work DCLab does not do.
- Exports keep branching on the task and write a plausible but wrong notebook for a kind that defines its own target.
- The Solution validator and the engine resolve the kind in two places, one without the pack, and disagree about which fields a solution may carry.

(5) How you will know it is done
- behaviour parity on eight projects: Stage records identical before and after, ids and timings normalised, with the run-to-run noise of two baseline runs as the reference.

- The final stage refuses when the holdout it would read is not the one the data stage locked. Because: The machine recomputes its split from the table; a lock must be checked, not assumed.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Each kind is called supported only when it reaches a careful data scientist's decisions on a synthetic replica of a realistic case; the Domain packs page must show that, generated, not hand-written maturity labels.

(2) Plan
1. Give the interface two hooks: case(seed) (the replica as a person brings it) and accept(run) (the decisions, each checked on the finished stage records).
2. Write a harness that builds the project the way a person would: attach the data and the label file, accept the agent's proposal, write the prediction moment, tick the columns the moment's own words name as written later.
3. Use the existing replicas (fraud, tickets, delivery) and write two new ones in dclab_core: subscription churn (binary) and product reviews (text), each with its traps.
4. Store the results with make kinds-check; build the matrix from the file; label the packs from the matrix and remove the hand-written labels.
5. Test the matrix logic (a failure turns a row partial, a forged 'supported' with a failing check is partial, a never-run kind is partial) and that the committed file matches a fresh run.

(3) Decisions
- Decisions are checked on the engine's own records (roles of columns, the split description, the metric, the holdout against the stage's baselines), never on a separate computation. Because: The acceptance must judge what DCLab decided, not what a test recomputes.
- Thresholds are principled margins (0.1 above chance or the majority, MAE at most 0.9 times the median's) rather than fitted to the first run. Because: A threshold tuned to the run passes by construction and says nothing.
- The matrix trusts no stored 'supported': it recounts the checks. Because: A result file edited by hand or a partial failure must never show as supported.
- The fraud case runs on the full engine (not quick), in its own test file. Because: Quick mode samples 3000 rows and leaves too few frauds; its own file lets the parallel runner start it first.

- The harness acts as a person who does more than the product offers, such as ticking proposals the page shows unticked, so a kind passes on the harness's diligence.
- A replica is so easy that a leaked column looks like skill, and a leak decision passes.
- A decision check reads a sentence the code always writes, so it can never fail.
- The matrix trusts a stored 'supported' that was edited by hand or written by a run that partly failed.
- Running the acceptance outside make sends stage records to a configured live model.

(5) How you will know it is done
- kind acceptance on replicas: Each decision of each kind holds on its replica (fixed with the kind before its first run): rare event 7 decisions, text 6, binary 6, multiclass 6, regression 5.

A finding (test, leakage): On the ticket replica, first_response_minutes stayed a model feature although it is known only after the queue answers.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Let DCLab solve forecasting problems: many series, a horizon and a forecast moment, judged on rolling origins that never see the future, with covariates kept to those known at the moment.

(2) Plan
1. Write the machine in dclab_core (pure: numpy, pandas, scikit-learn) so the main product can install it as it is.
2. Build a replica with the traps planted: a planned promotion known ahead, the day's rain measured on the day, a weekly season, short series.

(3) Decisions

The request: Let DCLab group customers that behave alike when there is no outcome to predict, and say honestly what such groups are worth.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Let DCLab group customers that behave alike when there is no outcome to predict, and say honestly what such groups are worth.

(2) Plan
1. Record every preprocessing choice: scale, logs, one-hot weights, what is left out and why.
2. For each k and method, refit on bootstrap resamples and measure agreement with the full fit; keep a k only when the interval's lower end holds.
3. Require separation beyond what the same method finds on data with no groups, so a stable split of a flat table is not called segments.
4. Leave out columns no plausible grouping uses, then search again; profile each segment in the data's own columns.
5. Review, fix, and show each test fails on the fault it guards.

(3) Decisions
- Stability is necessary but not enough: a k must also be better separated than on data with no groups. Because: k-means splits a flat square into four quadrants stably every time; stable is not the same as grouped.
- The null is a Gaussian with the data's spread and a flat box over its ranges, not the columns shuffled. Because: Shuffling keeps each column's shape, so groups that live in one column's two humps looked like no groups at all.
- A column is left out only when no plausible grouping (stable, separated, near the best silhouette) uses it. Because: Judging columns by the first choice alone, usually k=2, dropped the column that tells the two smaller groups apart; judging by every grouping kept a noise column a fine split had sliced.
- The record states there is no ground truth, and a named outcome only describes the segments. Because: A segmentation that predicts an outcome well is a different problem; the outcome never forms the groups.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Segments reported in data with no groups.
- A real signal column dropped as noise.
- An outcome used to form the segments.
- Segments presented as if they had a ground truth.

(1) What the package is for
Let DCLab find who changes because of an action (an offer, a call), not who would have bought anyway, and never call a difference an effect when the data cannot support it.

(2) Plan
1. Check how alike the arms are first: a propensity model out of fold, its AUC, the share of rows with comparable rows in the other arm, and imbalanced columns.
2. Bind the record's wording to that check and to the person's statement of randomisation.
3. Fit T- and X-learners and a transformed-outcome tree; compare them with a response model and random targeting.

- The observational campaign is a second table the person brings, said not random. Because: Generating it inside solve from the replica's seed would read the answer key.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Differences called effects without randomisation or overlap.
- A model chosen for finding who was targeted.
- A model chosen on the window it is reported on.
- Uplift confused with the chance of buying.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Let DCLab answer questions asked about an entity at a moment, from several related tables: will this customer stop ordering in the 30 days after a date, from customers, orders and tickets.

(2) Plan
1. Make one training row per (entity, cutoff); everything about a row from events strictly before its cutoff, its target from the horizon after it.
2. Check every join for repeated rows before it happens, and refuse with the numbers.
3. Find entity columns written at the export, not at any cutoff.

(3) Decisions
- Features stop strictly before the cutoff; the target window is [cutoff, cutoff + horizon). Because: With features before and the target after, an order on the cutoff day fell into neither, and every such order was lost.

Because: A row 15 days before the last cutoff reads 15 days of the holdout's own window as its target; checking the planned horizon instead of what was read let a doubled horizon pass.
- Entity numbers are compared with whole-log totals and last event times over the entities that have both. Because: A total exported with gaps made the correlation NaN and silently passed; a date stored as a number was never checked.
- A label table joins only before its label's time, or is refused when an entity has several cutoffs. Because: A June row of a customer whose churn was decided in March reads behaviour after the outcome.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Events after a row's cutoff in its features.
- Training targets read in the holdout's window.
- Columns of an export-day snapshot used as if known at a cutoff.
- Joins that repeat rows.

  Fix to ask for: Refuse non-finite numbers in every contract and test the JSON round trip of all six.

  Scenario: A non-Python host validating {'task': {'value': 'foo', 'status': 'stated'}} against problem_brief.json accepted it; Python refused it.

  Scenario: Under pydantic 2.5 and 2.9 all six schemas differed from the published files (the version literal gained an enum); with pydantic>=2.5 declared, the freshness test fails in such an environment.

  Fix to ask for: Declare pydantic>=2.10 and pin it in the R&D requirements.

Do a first data analysis that leads to decisions for binary, multiclass and regression alike: each finding with its evidence and what it implies for the plan, reading the target only on the training rows.

(2) Plan
1. Write the two replicas with their traps: tickets (tiny classes, a label copy resolved_by, duplicated tickets, a late class, a post-moment column) and delivery time (a cap at 60, a heavy tail, a target recomputable from timestamps, a post-delivery rating, negative distances, weather missing in storms, restaurants).

(3) Decisions
- Every claim about the target is measured out of fold (two seeded halves) against chance. Because: A column or entity that only memorises rows must not look like signal; shuffled labels must raise nothing.

- Ids are compared as text, never through float. Because: Long ids lose digits in a float and two ids collapse into one key.

- F1 [leakage] A holdout statistic steered a choice.
  Scenario: Training rows 100 to 149 had no conflicting groups and the holdout rows had two; the result reported groups: 2, and that finding bears on the primary metric.
  Why it matters: When the only conflicting groups sat in the holdout, the analysis still reported them from holdout labels, and that finding bears on the primary metric; the metric choice would then depend on rows the model is later judged on, breaking the train-only rule inside the analysis itself.
  Fix to ask for: Conflicting labels are counted on the training rows only; only target-free checks (duplicates, keys) use all rows.
- F2 [leakage] An exact copy of a multiclass label went unreported when one class held half the rows or more.
  Scenario: Classes at 70/20/10 and a column status_code equal to the label: power 0.294, no finding at all.
  Why it matters: On a ticket table where one team takes most tickets, a column that copies the team label raised no finding at all; a plan would keep it as a feature and the holdout score would look nearly perfect for a model that only reads the answer.
  Fix to ask for: Normalise the gain to (acc - majority) / (1 - majority).
- F3 [behaviour] Entity concentration fired on random labels.
  Scenario: With the fraud labels shuffled, biker_id was still a warning that labels concentrate (64 bikers with positives out of 240); on tickets mean purity was 0.533 under shuffled labels, above the 0.5 cut-off. The test of frauds on bikers proved nothing.

  Fix to ask for: Use the same out-of-fold power for entities as for columns, with a margin over chance, for every task.
- F5 [behaviour] analyse() raised on ordinary input.
  Scenario: Columns named 'Order Time' and 'Delivered At' gave an id with spaces that the contract refused; a key 'Customer ID' did the same; 600 classes made a statement over 4,000 characters; 40 disagreeing columns exceeded the 30-key limit; a regression with no labelled training rows put NaN in the evidence.
  Why it matters: A real export with spaced column names, hundreds of classes or dozens of disagreeing columns made analyse() raise instead of returning findings, so a host would fail at the first step of the workflow on ordinary data.
  Fix to ask for: Every id through one slug function, every list capped with 'and N more', no distribution finding without values.

- A plain prompted model is a third reader, scored the same way. Because: It shows what the quote check and the rules add over taking a model's answer as it comes.
- Dev runs first; the sealed set waits for the review's harness fixes. Because: The sealed set runs once; a harness bug found after it would waste it.

3. Make each proposal a test that code runs exactly as a telling name is tested, in its own slots, so it can add suspicion and never clear a finding.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
A training example should be able to carry a table without carrying a person's rows. A data card describes every table that reaches DCLab, and a synthetic table is drawn from the card with the same roles, relations and planted problems.

(2) Plan
1. Bands in one module (dclab_core.bands) so a card and a decision's state band a column the same way.
2. Relations measured on the source: key, join, disjoint, agrees, equals, null_when, one_to_one. Problems are derived from them, never from values.
3. A draw that rebuilds each column from its card, then applies the relations, and copies the label table's matched rows from the invented main table.

(3) Decisions
- Category names become codes (status_a, status_b) unless the caller keeps them for a public or synthetic table. Because: A category can be a person's name, a city or a shop.
- Numeric identifiers are drawn above the source's largest value. Because: A drawn id that equals a source id would point at a real customer or account.
- The traps are found as relations and problems, not declared by the replica. Because: The same card can then find them in a person's own tables.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A rounded quantile still says roughly where values lie: the scale of a fare, the city of the coordinates.
- Relations across rows (a behaviour, a formula between numbers) are not drawn again.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each fix undone fails a test
- wide table card time: a card of 100,000 rows and 25 id columns well under the 84.5 s measured

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Store and collect everything a person does in DCLab and everything DCLab does in reply, organized and findable.

(2) Plan
1. One record() reading its ids from the context; a file log by day and visit, a PostgreSQL table with a trigger refusing update and delete.
2. Mint the visit in the workspace middleware, carry the visit and request into jobs.
3. Hook the central writers once each, mapping their records onto the vocabulary, never failing them.
4. Test one real flow end to end; list every write route with what it records.
5. Review, read real row shapes, plant faults.

(3) Decisions
- Existing stores keep their jobs and emit into the log; nothing is rewritten. Because: Their readers (pages, trajectories, SFT) depend on them; the log joins them by ids.
- A visit's start is recorded with its first event, by the web process that minted it. Because: Pollers and probes would otherwise make a visit and a file per request; a worker must never repeat a start.
- Prompts and replies are kept only with DCLAB_LOG_PROMPTS=1, and never for a purpose shown cell values. Because: The usage log's own switch; a prompt holding sample rows would be cell values under a lower class.
- One action is one event: the draft's upload and save are the events; the build's copies are not. Because: Duplicates inflated uploads threefold and saves twofold.
- Every write route is listed with what it records or why nothing; a new route fails the test until it is. Because: Coverage is a decision per route, not an omission.
- The table is indexed by every id; partitioning by month is left for when a workspace's volume needs it. Because: Indexes serve the finder now; partitions are an operations choice.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Values exported through a shareable field.
- Duplicated events inflating counts.
- A visit per poll.
- A migration that changes or aborts.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each of the 6 planted faults in the recorder fails a test
- file and PostgreSQL: the same flow gives the same pinned event sequence on both stores
- the gate: rd-check, the suite on PostgreSQL, the agent environment's tests and the end-to-end flows pass

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner asked for everything that happens in DCLab to be stored in an organized, structured way that is clean and clear to find and understand; milestone A starts with finding and reading sessions.

(2) Plan
1. Give both logs (files and PostgreSQL) the same filters: person, kinds, a UTC window with the end excluded, many visits at once.
2. A finder over them: kinds, families and two groups (refused, errors) matching the session card; words only in what people and agents wrote; whole codes.
3. What a page shows: cell values never, model text only on request, people by name never by e-mail.

(3) Decisions
- A new permission 'timelines' held by the owner only, rather than reusing 'admin'. Because: The plan says owner and admin roles read timelines (proposed); 'admin' means changing settings and its refusal says so. A separate name lets the owner widen it later without widening settings.
- Words are searched in meta, person text and agent text; never in model text or a tool's values. Because: A search must not become a way to read what the page hides: prompts are kept only when the workspace keeps them, and a tool's arguments can hold a table's values.
- A code matches whole (case-insensitive), not as a part. Because: DCLAB-R1 must not find DCLAB-R17; a planted fault showed no test held this.
- The page's dates are the viewer's local days, sent as UTC times with the offset written out. Because: The page shows local times; a bare date was read as a UTC day, so evening events in the Americas and early-morning ones in Tehran fell on the wrong day.
- Refusals are filtered inside the read (SQL on PostgreSQL), not after it. Because: The 'refused' group reads every move and tool call; filtering afterwards let thousands of allowed moves fill the read's limit and hide older refusals.
- Error messages stay visible to the owner, as the contract classes them (agent text). Because: They are what explains a failed session; the contract notes a message may quote a value, and retention and redaction for export come with 19.10.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Who else reads timelines is still the owner's decision.
- A search reads the newest 20,000 events and says so; older ones need a date range.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each planted fault in the finder, the logs, the routes and the roles fails a test on its backend
- page in the browser: the owner's dev workspace reads as what happened: search, timeline, links, 375 px without sideways scroll, no console error

The request: The owner asked for every processing step to be stored in an organized way that is clear to find and understand; milestone A's second package makes every number traceable to the run, inputs and code that made it.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner asked for every processing step to be stored in an organized way that is clear to find and understand; milestone A's second package makes every number traceable to the run, inputs and code that made it.

(2) Plan
1. A RunRecord contract in dclab_core with a fingerprint of inputs and parameters, numbers by record path, a comparison of two runs, and the flat parts for the session record.
2. Move the event contract to v2 for the new kind run.recorded; read stored v1 events as v2.
3. The engine gives each stage run an id bound to every event inside it and writes its record into the stage record; failed and stopped runs too.
4. Agent runs (agents.run) and draft data pipelines as runs, through hooks that do nothing when no record is kept.
5. Trace a report path to its value and run with the report's own lookup; replay a stage in a scratch copy and refuse when anything it read differs.
6. Map the main product's experiments, stage runs and agent runs onto the same record; review, plant faults, fix.

(3) Decisions
- The event contract moves to v2 for one new kind; ExperienceEvent.read reads v1 as v2. Because: The kind is an enum in the frozen schema: a new kind changes its shape, and the rule is that a shape changes only with its version. Every v1 event is a valid v2 event, and the log is append-only, so stored rows are read, never rewritten.
- The run record lives with the host (the stage record here); the session record carries its flat parts. Because: The event vocabulary keeps meta flat and short; the full record (every number by path) belongs next to the evidence it describes.
- A replay reproduces a run or refuses: anything it would read differently (table, sampling, solution, run-changing settings, earlier choices, labels, pack, feature programs, plan, the engine profile) refuses it. Because: A replay under changed inputs would be a new run that nobody asked for; for the final stage it would be an uncounted, unaudited second look at the holdout.
- The final stage is replayed only on the code it ran on (same commit and the same uncommitted difference, by hash). Because: It reads the holdout: on the same code and inputs it can only repeat its number; on other code it would be a new evaluation.
- Only the settings that change a run enter its inputs (rows, quick, folds, the critic, private). Because: Turning the training opt-in on made a faithful replay look like a different run.
- The commit comes from git, or from DCLAB_COMMIT baked into the image. Because: The container has no .git: every deployed run would have recorded no code version.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Stage records from before 19.5 have no run; they say so until rerun.
- A label file held only in S3 is not copied into a replay's scratch folder.
- The run block adds about 25 KB to a final stage record (its numbers by path).

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each planted fault in the contract, the engine, replay, trace, hooks and the adapter fails a test
- report numbers traced: every number of a real solution report resolves to its value, and to its stage's run when a stage wrote it
- replays reproduce: models and final replayed in a scratch copy give the same value, choice and every number; the project unchanged

The request: The owner asked for every decision and step to be stored as training data for decision models of any kind (open-source fine-tuned, classical, hosted like Jev), in two uses: for data scientists and inside DCLab's workflow.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner asked for every decision and step to be stored as training data for decision models of any kind (open-source fine-tuned, classical, hosted like Jev), in two uses: for data scientists and inside DCLab's workflow.

(2) Plan
1. Read the main product's Jev at the recorded commit: its bands, its purposes, its acting bands, its answer row and its decision records.
2. One vocabulary of points (technical and workflow), each naming the main product's governed point, Jev's purpose and the plan's key.
3. A state of declared fields only (Jev's bands where Jev has the field); answers, options and labels checked against the point's answer shape.
4. Adapters both ways for Jev's rows; decision records at their points from the facts their services write.
5. Review, plant faults, fix.

(3) Decisions
- The state is a closed vocabulary of typed fields, not free metadata. Because: It is what a decision model trains on: anything open could carry a row's value; Jev's own bands are reused so a model trained here answers there on the same inputs.
- Names are allowed in the state as stored. Because: A column's name is what Jev sends too (as untrusted text); refusing names would make the identifier and leakage points unanswerable. Counts and measures can only be aggregates by the caller's discipline: stated as a limit.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner asked that every decision and step be stored as training data for decision models of any kind, for data scientists and inside DCLab's workflow, organized and findable.

(2) Plan
1. Map where each of the 45 points is decided in the studio (a subagent's survey of the code).
2. A ledger store like the session record: files or PostgreSQL (migration 0016), append-only, best effort, quiet during a replay.
3. One capture module: the saved solution against the proposal, the stages' choices, the graph's moves, Home's pack, workflow, question and card, cleaning, label joins, agents' tools and stops, the report's sentences, lessons.

(3) Decisions
- A saved solution is captured against the proposal made for its target, column by column. Because: That one moment holds the rule's answer and the person's for the identifier, leakage, time, group and task points: the richest decisions in the studio.
- A studied sample's written solution is planted truth: a benchmark label, never an answer. Because: Merged into the proposal, it made the rules look as right as the R&D's own solution; as labels it is what a decision model is measured against.
- A state never holds the decision's own value or the verdict it led to. Because: A model trained on the state would read its label there (the task in task.framing's state, the gate in a move's).
- A saved solution's records are written in one batch, off the event loop. Because: Hundreds of column decisions one transaction each would block the server on a remote database.
- The leakage stage's measured lift becomes a measured label of the person's forbidding. Because: It is the evidence that the column would have inflated the score: the best label the studio produces itself.
- Points not decided here are listed with why, and the list is checked complete. Because: A missing record must be a statement, never an omission; the owner's main product decides some of them.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Points for the unit, moment, entities and findings do not exist yet.
- The research campaign chooses on its own endpoint, outside the ledger.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each planted fault in the capture, the ledger and their call sites fails a test
- Home to the stages: every point decided on the path leaves a record with its answers, none holding a table value

The request: The owner wants the sessions worth reading found without reading them all, and wants their failures turned into benchmark cases. The morning when an anomaly-detection draft was built as a model of customer ids should be found by rule, by more than one detector.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner wants the sessions worth reading found without reading them all, and wants their failures turned into benchmark cases. The morning when an anomaly-detection draft was built as a model of customer ids should be found by rule, by more than one detector.

(2) Plan
1. Detectors as pure rules over the shared event contract, so the main product can run the same ones on its own rows.
2. One read per visit, shared by the card and its flags.
3. Feedback as an event of kind feedback.given; on a yes or no decision, also a user_decision_exposed label saying the opposite.

(3) Decisions
- The data analysis's role for a column wins over its name. Because: country_code analysed as categorical is a category. A name is only a guess, so a hit on the name alone is medium severity, not high.
- Only blocking questions count for built_with_question_open, tracked per conversation. Because: Home lets a build go past the unit and action questions on purpose (dclab_core.card, blocks=False). An answer given in another conversation does not answer this one.
- A question asked again with different options is a follow-up, not a repeat. Because: Home asks for the outcome in words first, then asks again with the column options once the data arrives. That is the main flow, not a failure.
- Only someone who may change the work or review it turns "wrong" into a label, and only once. Because: A label weighs on what the decision models learn. A viewer's opinion is kept as feedback; duplicates would inflate the counts.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The card reads at most 5000 events a visit and the timeline 20000, so a very long visit's flags can differ between the two.
- The detectors are rules: their precision on real sessions is not yet measured (19.12 turns flagged sessions into benchmark cases).

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each fix undone fails a test
- the owner's morning: flagged by at least two detectors

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
PostgreSQL only, for a team of about 1,000 users, runnable locally and later in the cloud. Build the schema and migrations and a PostgreSQL implementation of the 9.1 storage interfaces, tested against a real database, never a mock.

(2) Plan
1. Ask the owner before touching the local PostgreSQL server: create two new databases (dclab_dev for working data, dclab_test for the tests, which empty it) and install the psycopg driver.
2. Write the schema: ten tables (workspace, app_user, membership, project, stage_record, activity, transition, draft, draft_event, intern_session) and the first migration; python -m dclab_rnd.storage upgrade.
3. Share the 'new document' builders between the file and PostgreSQL stores so both create identical documents.
4. Write the PostgreSQL stores: row locks for update, draft event numbers from an UPDATE of the draft row, the agent turn as an advisory lock, every query filtered by workspace.
5. Write one contract test that runs the same behaviours against both backends.
6. Switch the server with DCLAB_DATABASE_URL; run the whole suite on PostgreSQL and on files, and make product-e2e on PostgreSQL.
7. Measure a page of 50 projects among 10,000 with timings and the query plan; add a test that the migration and the models describe the same database; add make test-pg.

(3) Decisions
- Two fixed databases on the developer's machine: dclab_dev and dclab_test. Because: The tests empty their database; sharing one with working data would delete the owner's projects on every test run. A temporary database per run needs create and drop rights and can leave strays after a crash. The owner asked why two and agreed.
- A document read whole is JSONB; what a list filters or sorts on is a column with an index. Because: Stage records, solutions and drafts are always read whole, while lists need indexed workspace, status and time columns to stay fast at thousands of projects.
- Keep the file stores and switch with one setting. Because: Both backends stay tested by the same suite and contract test, and a laptop without PostgreSQL still runs.
- Each workspace folder is one workspace until accounts exist. Because: Accounts come in 10.2; until then the folder is the only identity a request has, and isolation can already be tested per workspace.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Tests that empty their database would delete the owner's projects if they shared it with working data.
- An upsert guarded by a WHERE clause can look successful when it wrote nothing.
- Two backends can disagree silently (strict against lenient JSON) unless one contract test runs on both.
- A lock held in one process means nothing to another: updates, draft event numbers and agent turns need locks in the database.
- Lists that filter or sort inside JSON documents slow down at thousands of projects without indexed columns.

(5) How you will know it is done
- projects list at 10,000 projects: The projects list stays fast with 10,000 projects, measured with the query plan (the package's Done when).
- results unchanged by the storage backend: The whole suite and make product-e2e pass on PostgreSQL with the same results as on files.

The upsert returns the saved id (RETURNING); no id back means the row belongs to another workspace, and save raises KeyError.
